title.rendered: When We Aim God’s Lightning Toward Other People

content.rendered:
What if the God you were taught to fear is still shaping the way you see other people?

I often think about the moment, now more than six decades ago, when I opened our family Bible and saw God staring back at me.

It terrified me.

He stood on the clouds with a scowl on His face. But it was His eyes that made me tremble. Lightning bolts shot from them, and in my young mind, they seemed aimed directly at me.

No wonder I slammed the cover shut and ran for cover.

For years, I thought the damage from that picture was mostly personal. It made me afraid of God.

I was wrong.

It took me decades to understand the greater danger.

A frightening picture of God does more than frighten the person who believes it. When we become convinced that God looks at certain people with anger, disgust, or condemnation, sooner or later we may begin looking at them the same way.

Once we believe God has rejected someone, it becomes much easier for us to reject them too.

We exclude.

We shame.

We point fingers.

We decide who belongs and who does not.

That realization eventually found its way into A God Awful God:

“The lightning had not stayed inside the picture. We had learned to aim it at people.”

Who did your church teach you God was angry with?

Who were you warned about?

Who was described as dangerous, sinful, rebellious, deceived, or outside the reach of God’s love?

In my story, one of the groups eventually caught in that lightning was the LGBTQ community. But the pattern is much larger than one issue.

Churches have aimed it at doubters, divorced people, women who would not stay in their assigned roles, people who left the church, people who asked forbidden questions, and anyone who made certainty uncomfortable.

Maybe the important question is not only, “What do I believe about God?”

Maybe it is also, “What kind of person is my picture of God teaching me to become?”

A God Awful God is the story of how my picture of God changed and what happened when that change began rearranging the way I saw other people.

The manuscript is now finished and moving into production.

title.rendered: What If You Gave Yourself Permission to Ask?

content.rendered:
Have you ever had a question you were afraid to ask?

I’m not talking about school days when you finally raised your hand and started with, “This might be a dumb question…” only to hear the teacher say, “There’s no such thing as a dumb question.”

I mean a question that, if answered honestly, might change your world.

Maybe it was a question about God.
Maybe it was a question about the church.
Maybe it was a Bible story you had heard your entire life but suddenly saw in a troubling new light.

You had a question and were afraid to ask it, not because you thought it was stupid, but because you realized where it might lead.

Growing up in the church, I knew that fear well.

I was taught that having faith meant having answers. Good Christians had answers. Successful pastors had even more answers. And, of course, if there was no plausible answer at all, we were told to take it by faith.

It was okay to ask questions as long as they pointed you back to what we already knew.

I learned the hard way that there were acceptable answers and there were right answers. Too often, they were not the same thing.

While in seminary, I took a class on the book of Isaiah from a very conservative professor. We explored the authorship of Isaiah. Conservative scholars argued for one author. Less conservative scholars argued for two. Liberal scholars made the case for three.

At the end of the semester, we were asked to write an essay answering a simple question: How many authors wrote Isaiah?

I had studied hard. I knew what I believed. I made the case for three authors.

I knew it was risky because the professor was very conservative. But I assumed he would grade me on my knowledge and the strength of my argument.

When my paper was returned, I was stunned. A large red C glared back at me.

I had taken several classes from this professor. On every test and assignment, I had earned an A or a B.

There were no corrections on my paper. No comments. No explanation.

Then it hit me.

I had not given the acceptable answer.

Maybe you learned the same lesson in a different way.

When you asked a question, someone changed the subject.

A pastor warned you not to “go down that road.”

A Sunday School teacher told you to take it by faith.

Someone made it clear there could be a price for asking the wrong question.

You didn’t get a C on a test, but you learned the lesson. There were acceptable answers and there were right answers. Eventually, you started editing your own questions before opening your mouth.

So what questions are you afraid to ask out loud?

Are you afraid to ask how the God of the Old Testament can sometimes appear so bloodthirsty?

Are you afraid to ask what happened to someone you loved after they died?

Are you afraid to ask whether the Bible is really infallible?

Are you afraid to ask whether the church might be wrong about something you were told could never be questioned?

Giving yourself permission to ask can feel dangerous. It can feel like stepping onto thin ice and hearing it crack beneath your feet.

But I have also discovered something else. Sometimes the question you are most afraid to ask is the one that finally sets you free.

A God Awful God: The God I Feared Wasn’t The God I Found is the story of the questions I was afraid to ask, and what happened when I finally gave myself permission to ask them.

Near the end of the book, I imagine talking to the frightened little boy I once was. I tell him what I wish someone had told me much earlier: questions are not dangerous.

title.rendered: Do You Worship a God-Awful God?

content.rendered:
In my upcoming memoir, I wrote this line:

“God could be a God-awful God.”

Have you ever thought God was awful?

Be honest.

If you can’t be honest, why not? Do you fear God will punish you? Are you afraid that even thinking those words might put you in jeopardy?

If you answered yes to either question, you may be worshiping a God defined by fear.

I don’t blame you. It may be the God you were taught to believe in.

As a young child, perhaps your Sunday School teacher taught you the story of Noah and the ark. In that story, God becomes so angry that He kills the entire population except Noah and his family. Why does He kill everyone else? Because they were bad and made Him angry.

At that age, you may not have connected all the dots. But perhaps you wondered how a loving God could drown all those people.

In your teenage years, you read the Bible as instructed. You began noticing other troubling stories like the one about Uzzah and the Ark of the Covenant.

When the oxen stumbled, the Ark lurched. Uzzah thought it was going to fall, so he reached out to steady it.

Boom.

God struck him dead.

As you grew older and listened more attentively to sermons, you began noticing words wrapped in fear. You were told that if you didn’t stop doing bad things or start doing good ones, you were in trouble. You were a sinner, and sinners went to hell—to burn forever and ever.

Eternally.

And perhaps you began to wonder: Is this a God I should run toward or run from?

Have you ever stood beside the casket of a loved one during a funeral visitation? Well-meaning people file past and try to console you. One person says, “We don’t know why God took your daughter, but we know He has a plan.” Another softly assures you that your son is in heaven because God needed another tenor in the angelic choir.

Did your anger at God rise to the level of an inner scream?

It wasn’t only the church that reinforced this frightening picture. We still use the phrase “acts of God” to describe hurricanes, tornadoes, floods, earthquakes, and other disasters that destroy homes and kill people.

There it was again. That subtle suggestion that God could be a God-awful God.

“God could be a God-awful God.”

I wrote that sentence in my memoir. I didn’t write it because I believe God is awful. I wrote it because the God I was taught to fear often appeared to be.

But don’t overlook the subtitle. It does some heavy lifting:

The God I Feared Wasn’t the God I Found.

After nearly forty years of ministry and a lifetime of study, I began to see that the God I feared didn’t exist. That frightening image had been created by misinformation and people who meant well. Sometimes it was shaped by people who used the fear of God as a motivational tool to keep you in line or ensure that you gave money to the church.

I discovered that it takes years to shed the fear of God. But once I embraced the boundless love of God, fear ran for a place to hide and found none.

That’s why I wrote my memoir. It isn’t because my life is special. It is because my story traces a transformation from fearing God to loving Him.

title.rendered: What If the God You Fear Looks Like Someone From Your Past?

content.rendered:
I was seven years old when the church gave God a name I feared: Father.

Looking back, I realize that word was supposed to make me feel safe. It didn’t.

When my Sunday School teacher prayed, “Dear Heavenly Father,” it didn’t give me warm fuzzies. I pictured my dad standing over me with a leather belt ready to swing across my bare butt. “Father” meant anger. Terror. Danger. 

Decades later, I began to understand what had taken place in me. God didn’t create my fear. He inherited it.

Long before I knew what the word “theology” meant, I constructed an image of God. To build that image, I used the raw materials life had given me. 

At that early age, I knew what anger looked like and what unpredictable power felt like. I learned the wisdom of staying quiet, reading the room, and trying not to make my father angry.

Then the church told me God was my Father. So I filled in the blanks. 

I suspect we all do this.

Centuries ago, the Greek philosopher Xenophanes wrote that people had a tendency to imagine that the gods looked like themselves. His observation sparked writers to say that rather than God creating us in his image, we create God in ours.

But I think we do more than shape God in our image. We give Him our history.

If the people who held power in our lives were gentle, we may find it easy to imagine a gentle God. If we felt loved and valued in our childhood, trusting divine love may come naturally. But if authority was scary, unpredictable, controlling, or conditional, those experiences often follow us right into church.

We might hear a Sunday School teacher say, “God is watching us.” Because of our experiences, we imagine a God watching from afar, not caring for us, but waiting for us to mess up. 

If we hear the preacher say that God judges us, we imagine someone waiting for us to fail so the leather belt can be applied.

When someone begins their prayer with “Heavenly Father,” we unknowingly attach an earthly father’s face to the word. And we shrink back.

As we live with this picture of God created by fear, something strange happens.

We start defending our picture of God as though God Himself painted it.

That thought eventually forced me to ask one of the most important questions of my life: What if some of the things I believed about God had never belonged to God at all? Was God really like the power person in my life who terrified and controlled me?

That question sent me back to Jesus.

The God I saw in Jesus began reshaping the God I had feared.

Jesus moved toward wounded people instead of away from them. He touched people others avoided. He welcomed children. He ate with people the religious institution pushed aside. He seemed far more interested in healing people than scaring them.

Slowly, something changed.

I began taking things back from God that I had put on Him.

The anger.

The fear.

The lightning in His eyes.

And underneath all of that, I began discovering someone I had not expected.

This journey is at the heart of my upcoming memoir, A God Awful God: The God I Feared Wasn’t the God I Found.

If you’ve ever wondered whether the God you fear is really God or a picture assembled from things that happened to you, I wrote this book with people like us in mind.

title.rendered: My Silence Became Part of the Answer

content.rendered:
Fifteen-year-old Meg raised her left hand to ask a question. She sat cross-legged on the floor with the other teenagers. Her right hand gripped a piece of pepperoni pizza.

In a quiet voice, she looked at Dr. McGreely and asked, “Is my grandma in heaven? She died three months ago, and I’m worried. She didn’t attend church.”

Pastor McGreely was a visiting speaker at our church. His church was the largest in our denomination in the entire state. In every sense of the phrase, he was a rock star.

This was an informal question-and-answer session with the church teenagers. Meg had never been to our church before.

McGreely turned and looked at her. He scrunched up his face and replied, “Well, if she didn’t go to church, she wasn’t a Christian. That means she’s in hell.”

He paused for a moment and asked, “Does anyone else have a question?”

Meg’s head dropped toward her chest. One of the girls reached over and patted her knee. I heard Meg sniffle as she fought back tears.

He had dropped a bomb into her life. Every teenager in the room felt the impact.

He could have said, “Only God makes decisions like that.” He could have said, “God knows her heart.”

But the preacher with the Bible on the table beside him had delivered his verdict.

Hell.

Meg’s grandmother was, at that very moment, burning forever in the Lake of Fire.

I thought I might throw up.

I stood in the back of the room and watched it happen. I knew I should say something. But I reminded myself that he was the professional and I was the amateur. This early in my career, openly disagreeing with one of our denomination’s most prominent preachers could be dangerous.

From the back of the room, I watched Meg’s head and shoulders curl forward. Her body shook with silent sobs.

And I just stood there.

I wanted to tell her that God loved her grandma. I should have told her that only God gets to make the heaven-or-hell decision. Only God knew her heart. I needed to tell her that going to church and loving God were two very different things.

But I stood there silently.

I was silent because I was afraid.

I hadn’t pronounced an eternity in hell upon Meg’s grandma. I hadn’t said the words. I wasn’t the one who had caused her to sob. I hadn’t dropped that bomb into her life.

But I didn’t challenge McGreely’s verdict.

My silence became part of the answer she received.

The next Sunday, I watched for her.

No Meg.

The following week, I searched the congregation again.

No Meg.

She never came back.

Over the years, I have often wondered what happened to her. I have carried the shame of that afternoon with me. I allowed fear of denominational displeasure to force me into silence.

For years, I tried to understand why I said nothing. Of course, I had plenty of excuses. But the real reason still bothers me.

I was protecting myself.

I didn’t want people to think I had disrespected the visiting preacher. I didn’t want my challenge to his theology to suggest that I didn’t understand the Bible.

So when Meg needed me, I chose silence.

Religious harm isn’t caused only by people who say cruel things in God’s name. Sometimes it is propped up by those of us who remain silent when we should speak.

We tell ourselves the time isn’t right.

We don’t want to create trouble.

We hope someone else will speak.

We may even convince ourselves that remaining quiet is the loving thing to do.

Sometimes silence is the wise choice. We don’t need to accept every invitation to a fight.

But silence is not always neutral.

Sometimes silence tells a frightened teenager that the cruel answer must be true.

Sometimes it tells an LGBTQ+ person that no one in the room will stand beside them.

Sometimes it tells a woman that her calling will always matter less than her gender.

Sometimes silence tells a person wounded by the church that protecting the institution is more important than protecting them.

I wish I could return to that room.

I wish I could stand beside Meg and say, “No one gets to place your grandma beyond the reach of God’s love.”

I can’t change what happened that day. It is too late to give Meg the answer I should have given her.

But I can refuse to remain silent now.

Maybe that is the difficult gift of regret. There are no do-overs. But we can decide that the next time someone needs a voice beside their own, we will speak.

I don’t know where Meg is today. But I hope she discovered that the answer she received in our church was not the only answer.

Maybe somewhere along the way, she found a God far more loving than the one we showed her.

This story comes from my upcoming memoir, A God Awful God: The God I Feared Wasn’t the God I Found. If you are questioning fear-based religion or searching for a more honest faith rooted in love, I invite you to join my book email list below. I’ll share occasional articles, book updates, and publication news.

Note: McGreely and Meg and pseudonyms to protect their identity.

title.rendered: I Learned How to Perform Certainty

content.rendered:
And I suspect I’m Not the Only One

As a pastor, I loved preaching. With a Bible in one hand and a pulpit in front of me, I could tell you what almost any verse meant.

I even knew what God thought.

Seminary training taught me to preach with conviction. Looking back, I can’t remember ever hearing a preacher begin a point with, “I think the Bible says…”

I once preached a sermon in which I became a cheap imitation of a high-dollar evangelist. I waved the Bible in the air. I strutted back and forth across the platform. I raised and lowered my voice at all the right moments.

I projected more certainty than I possessed.

After the sermon, a woman hurried up to me and gushed, “Oh, Pastor, I just loved your sermon.”

My chest swelled with unearned pride.

“What did I say that you liked?” I asked.

She stopped, thought, and smiled.

“I don’t know. I just liked how you said it.”

I had delivered certainty so convincingly that what I said hardly mattered.

Sometimes in the church world, certainty carries more authority than truth.

But preachers aren’t the only people who learn to perform certainty.

Maybe you learned to do it in Sunday school, where every question had an answer printed in the teacher’s book. Maybe you nodded during a sermon while doubts lurked inside you. Maybe you repeated what your church believed because everyone around you repeated it too.

Maybe you sang words you were no longer sure you believed because the person beside you was singing them with eyes closed and hands raised.

Or perhaps you stayed silent when a Bible study turned toward hell, sexuality, suffering, or unanswered prayer because you knew your questions would make others uncomfortable.

We learn early that certainty belongs. It makes you part of the in-crowd.

Doubt makes people nervous. It builds fences.

I’ll let you in on a little secret: I wasn’t always completely certain about what I preached.

I had doubts. I had questions. But if certainty and conviction were the marks of a good preacher, doubts and questions seemed like evidence of a bad one.

So I learned how to perform certainty while uncertainty lived inside me.

This wasn’t conscious dishonesty. I wasn’t trying to fool anyone. I was part of a religious institution in which certainty was one of the highest virtues. If I didn’t fully understand the denomination’s interpretation of a passage, that didn’t give me permission to question it publicly.

My job was to proclaim the approved interpretation with confidence.

Most people who perform certainty aren’t trying to deceive anyone either.

We do it because we want to belong. You can no longer sit at the cool table.

We don’t want friends or family to worry about our souls. We don’t want our pastor to see us as a problem. We may be afraid that one honest question will lead to another. We are afraid of where those questions will take us.

The familiar answers may no longer feel true, but they still feel safe. They feel like home.

I eventually discovered that questions were acceptable as long as they led back to the approved church answers. You could wander around inside the fence, provided you never climbed over it.

But when your questions began leading somewhere else, you were no longer considered curious.

You were considered dangerous.

Performed certainty has a cost. We learn to mistrust the quiet voice that says, “This doesn’t make sense,” “This doesn’t seem loving,” or simply, “I’m not sure.”

It can also change how we treat other people. When protecting an answer becomes more important than understanding someone’s life, we stop listening. And we do that even when the person standing in front of us has been wounded by what we believe.

I haven’t stopped believing. I still have convictions about the Bible, God, love, justice, and what gives life meaning.

But I hold those convictions differently now.

I’ve learned to say, “This is what I believe, but I could be wrong.”

Those words once sounded weak. Now they sound honest. They leave room for another person’s story, for new understanding, and perhaps even for the voice of God.

If I stood behind a pulpit today, I would still speak with conviction. But I hope I would no longer confuse the volume of my voice with the truth of my words.

I once believed certainty was evidence of faith.

Now I wonder whether faith begins when we become honest about what we do not know.

Maybe you have questions you’ve kept behind the fence because you’re afraid of where they might lead.

Let them breathe.

You don’t have to perform certainty to belong.

And you don’t have to silence your questions to be faithful.

title.rendered: Where Does It Hurt?

content.rendered:
For almost forty years, I stood behind pulpits with an open Bible in front of me.

I loved the people sitting in the pews. I wanted them to know God. Whatever situation they faced, my goal was to help them with my words. 

But sometimes I hurt them.

I remember one Sunday when I preached about giving money to the church. I used the familiar passage from the Old Testament book of Malachi about robbing God. The message was simple. If you weren’t giving God what belonged to Him, you were stealing from Him.

I believed it.

Sitting in the congregation that morning was a man named Earl. He was struggling financially. Earl had stopped giving to the church, not because he didn’t want to give, but because he couldn’t. His recent divorce generated the need to provide large child support payments. 

I can still see him sitting there.

As I preached, his chin dropped. He looked down at his hands.

At the time, I probably interpreted his response as conviction.

Preachers learn to do that. Someone bows a head. Someone wipes away a tear or becomes quiet. We interpret that to mean God is at work using our words. It’s easy to think, “I’m getting through.” Or, “the Holy Spirit is using this sermon.”

It took me years to realize I might be wrong. There was another possibility.

Maybe Earl wasn’t convicted.

Maybe he was crushed.

He had walked into church carrying a huge financial load. Unpaid bills were stacking up. The shame of not being able to pay his weekly offerings to the church added to his stress. 

Then I stood in front of the congregation with an open Bible and told him he was robbing God.

Ouch.

I hadn’t meant to hurt him. That’s the part that bothers me most. I was trying to be faithful to my call to “preach the Word.”

As I’ve grown older, I’ve started looking differently at the Jesus I find in the Bible.

He seemed remarkably uninterested in making wounded people hurt more.

He touched people others considered outcasts. He let children get close. He ate with the outliers and heretics who made religious people uncomfortable. 

When a woman was dragged before Him and surrounded by people ready to condemn her, Jesus didn’t add another accusation. He didn’t share His favorite memory verse. He didn’t preach a sermon.

He got down in the dust.

In recent years, I’ve thought about that a lot. I started paying closer attention to Jesus. How did He treat the people who had screwed up? What about the people, religious folks had already judged? The people carrying secret buckets of pain?

I began to see something I had missed.

Fear taught me to ask, “What did they do wrong?”

Jesus seemed to ask, “Where does it hurt?”

When I saw him sitting in my congregation staring down at his hands, I wish I had asked Earl that question after church. 

Where does it hurt?

I can’t go back and change that sermon. There are other things from forty years of ministry I also can’t undo.

But I can decide which question I want to ask now.

When I meet someone who is struggling, wounded, doubting, divorced, angry at the church, frightened of God, or simply trying to survive, I don’t want my first question to be: What did they do wrong? I’ve asked that question enough.

These days, I’m trying to follow Jesus into a better question. 

Where does it hurt?

title.rendered: What If God Never Told Them to Kill?

content.rendered:
I plopped down in my easy chair in the living room. Ten minutes earlier I had rolled out of bed and made a cup of coffee. I stretched. Yawned. Put my bare feet up on the footstool.

I picked up the book I had been reading by Pete Enns. His books are not exactly on the approved reading list of my denomination. I didn’t care. I wanted a fresh perspective on what I had been taught about the Bible for more than six decades.

I sipped my coffee and turned to where I had stopped reading the day before.

And then something shifted.

Five years later, I realize that what happened that morning didn’t tear my faith apart. It opened it up.

In his book, Bible scholar Pete Enns discusses the story of the Israelites slaughtering the Canaanites. The story says God told them to kill every Canaanite—including the children and babies.

That’s a real problem if you want to believe God is love.

What do you do with a God who orders the murder of toddlers and babies?

It was a question I had tried to resolve during nearly 40 years of ministry. The story of God sending the flood and killing millions troubled me. The story of God sending the Death Angel to kill the oldest male child in every Egyptian house sent shivers down my back. And there are more stories in the Bible that made me wonder if God really was a God of love.

My eyes returned to the book in my hand.

Then I read this:

“These ancient writers had an adequate understanding of God for them in their time, but not for all time.”

I stopped.

Enns had just offered me another possibility concerning the Canaanites.

Maybe God didn’t command the Israelites to slaughter the Canaanites.

Perhaps the Israelites believed God had commanded it.

I stared at the page.

Maybe the Bible isn’t always true.

I held my breath. Closed my eyes. Waited.

No lightning bolt from heaven.

The possibility was unsettling: What if some biblical writers were describing their understanding of God from within their own time and culture? What if their understanding wasn’t necessarily the final word about God?

That question opened a door.

It gave me the freedom to think openly about some of the bloody stories of the Bible. Eventually, I began thinking differently about other passages too—including the verses used to condemn members of the gay community.

And that thinking put me on a collision course with the denomination I had given my life to.

What happened next—and what I eventually discovered about the God behind the Bible—is at the heart of “A God Awful God: The God I Feared Wasn’t the God I Found.”

title.rendered: The Day I Stopped Defending God

content.rendered:
Before the doors opened, I tried to prepare myself for what was about to happen. I looked around the unfamiliar room, appointed with an elegance unfamiliar to me. I noticed the nauseating smell of multiple kinds of flowers melded together. There were rows of chairs lined up expecting company. And then there was the casket.

I tried not to look. There was no need, but I looked anyhow. The casket was just five feet away. It was a powdery steel blue. Inside was my little brother. Mom had chosen a blue leisure suit for his final apparel. His long blond hair was meticulously arranged, as though hiding something.

Mike had just turned 18. In several months he would graduate from high school. But during a spring break trip to Cocoa Beach, Florida, he had been walking along a road. A drunk driver swerved and killed him. And now, here we were. Soon the doors would open and friends and family would enter the funeral home to pay their final respects.

We had grown up in the church. In this tough moment, my spiritual training assured me that God would help us. He would be there bringing comfort and strength.

As the doors to the visitation room opened and people walked in, it never occurred to me that God might be to blame.

It takes stamina to stand for hours next to the casket of your brother and shake hands with a fake smile plastered on your face. Mike was popular at school. As his friends filed past they had nothing to say. They just fought back tears and looked like they would rather be any place but there.

But I struggled with some of the comments from the church people I grew up with.

They meant well. But I wished they would stop talking. How many times did I need to hear, “God has a plan”? Why did they find it necessary to tell me, “We don’t know why God took him, but He knows what He’s doing”? Or, “Sometimes we just can’t figure out why He does the things He does”?

It didn’t hit me all at once. But it started to feel as though the church people were defending the actions of God. Based on what I heard, some of them believed my brother was dead because of God. They believed God was in control and because of that He could’ve saved my brother.

Even worse, it sounded like God might have been driving the car.

I began to wonder what to do with a God who needed defending at my brother’s casket. What about all those Bible verses that promise the protection of God? What do I say to people who brag about how good God is because He delivered them from sickness or bankruptcy or death?

What about my brother?

I glanced down inside the casket. It appeared as though God hadn’t been good to him.

At 23, I didn’t have another way to understand it. I had grown up believing God was on the side of good people. God protected us. God answered prayer. God wouldn’t let us down.

Standing beside Mike’s casket, that certainty began to crack.

I didn’t stop believing in God. But I carried those questions with me into seminary and eventually into pastoral ministry. And yet, during nearly forty years as a pastor, I can’t count how many times I repeated some of those same answers to hurting and grieving people.

I knew the lines. They were the lines Christians were supposed to say.

The church had taught me answers. It had not taught me what to do when the answers stopped working.

Eventually, I gave myself permission to ask the questions I had carried away from my brother’s casket. I began to think for myself and break free from worn-out church platitudes. Some of the answers I once believed didn’t survive those questions.

But God did.

When that happened, I began to see God differently.

That’s one of the reasons I wrote *A God Awful God: The God I Feared Wasn’t the God I Found.*

Nearly fifty years later, I can still see that powder-blue casket. I still don’t believe Mike’s death was part of some divine plan that needed defending.

And I no longer believe God needs me to defend Him.

title.rendered: The Noah’s Ark Story I Couldn’t Unsee

content.rendered:
I was nine years old, sitting cross-legged on the linoleum floor of our church basement.

Sister Shirley told us we had a really fun Bible story that morning. Noah and the ark.

I already knew enough about the story to like it. There was a huge boat, animals two by two, a dove carrying a branch and, eventually, a beautiful rainbow.

Sister Shirley told us the world had become terribly evil, so God decided to start over. Noah obeyed God, built the ark, gathered his family and the animals, and God shut the door.

Then the rain came.

In my imagination, I could see everything. The animals. The rising water. Noah and his family safely inside.

But then my mind added something Sister Shirley hadn’t mentioned. I heard pounding. Thud. Thud. Fists against the door of the ark.

Suddenly I understood something I had never considered before.

If Noah and his family were safely inside the ark, everybody else was outside.

And the door was locked.

That realization changed the story for me.

Until then, Noah’s ark had belonged in the same category as so many other childhood Bible stories. It was filled with colorful pictures, a hero and a lesson at the end about how much God loved us.

But once I thought about the people outside the boat, I couldn’t stop thinking about them.

What happened to the children? What happened to the babies? What had they done? What was their sin?

Then the most frightening question of all popped into my head. If God could become angry enough to do that to them, what kept Him from doing something terrible to me?

Those were scary questions for a nine-year-old. They were also questions I kept mostly to myself.

That’s the part of the story that interests me most today. Children often hear more than adults realize. An adult can hear a Bible story about judgment and then wrap it with theology and explanations accumulated over centuries.

A child doesn’t have any of that. A child hears, “God killed everybody.” Then the child tries to figure out what that tells him about God. I certainly did.

Sister Shirley eventually reached the happy ending. She showed us the rainbow and explained that it was God’s promise never to destroy the earth with a flood again.

Everyone seemed satisfied. I wasn’t.

The rainbow was pretty, but it couldn’t bring the millions of dead back to life.

For me, the rainbow didn’t erase the terrifying part of the story. In some ways it made the contradiction more obvious.

I was being told two things at once. 

God loves you. 

God can destroy you.

At nine years old, I didn’t know how to make those ideas live together. So I did what children often do. I became careful.

If God could become dangerously angry, then maybe my job was to make sure I never gave Him a reason to hurt me. Even at that young age I determined to be good, to obey. Don’t ask the wrong questions. Don’t get on the wrong side of the door.

Years later, I became a pastor. I spent decades talking about God, studying Scripture and trying to help other people believe that God loved them.

But the frightened boy in that church basement didn’t disappear just because the adult version of him learned theology.

That’s one of the things I’ve come to understand about religious fear. It doesn’t always present itself as fear. Sometimes it calls itself obedience. Or even holiness or faith.

For a long time, I thought being afraid of God meant I took God seriously. Today I’m not so sure. I also no longer think the answer to disturbing Bible stories is to pretend the disturbing parts aren’t there.

The nine-year-old boy sitting on that basement floor deserved something better than, “Don’t worry about that. Look at the pretty rainbow.”

He deserved permission to ask, Why? Or, What do I do when something I’ve been taught about God scares me?

Maybe some of our most important spiritual questions begin when we finally stop pretending that everything makes sense.

I still remember the rainbow from that Sunday School lesson.

But I also remember the water.

Maybe faith became more honest for me when I finally gave myself permission to look at both.

If this stirred something in you, you’re not alone that’s part of why I wrote the book. Enter your email below and I’ll send you Chapter 1 free right now.

title.rendered: Why the God We Fear as Children Can Follow Us for a Lifetime

content.rendered:
I have a relative who is terrified of clowns. To those of us who do not share the fear, it may seem almost comical. But to someone who imagines Bozo climbing into the car beside them, there is nothing funny about it.

Sometimes those fears can be traced to an early frightening encounter.

This is especially true if that thing is the Lord God Almighty.

Before my first encounter I had the impression God was like a cosmic Santa Claus. If I was nice He would give me good things. But if I spit on my brother, God would do bad things to me.

When I entered my living room at seven years of age I had never seen the family Bible there on the end table. It caught my attention that hot day as I came inside needing a cold drink after playing kickball. Maybe it had been there for a long time but there it was. I walked over, driven by curiosity and opened the front cover. 

There He was, my first picture of God. He didn’t look happy. He was angry. The stone tablets in each hand looked like weapons he could use to hit me in the head. But it was His eyes that captured my attention. They looked like lightening bolts shooting out into the room. And they followed me when I shifted my stance from foot to foot. 

That image stuck with me. It never let me go. To this day I can still feel the panic. 

At the age of seven I didn’t understand theology but I could feel emotion. In that picture God was watching me. He saw what I did and would do. His glare signaled His disapproval. Fear crept into my mind and body. I knew nothing about hell or eternal punishment. All I knew was that I might be in danger and I needed to be very careful.

Why do children embrace their early images of God? Maybe it’s because they trust the adults that introduce them to those images. In my case I knew the Bible arrived from my parents. Why would they have a Bible with a scary picture if it didn’t represent God? It never occurred to me that my parents or the artist had an erroneous understanding of God. 

Young children often have little ability to separate symbol from reality, especially if the image is wrapped in religious authority. If an adult saw God in a picture like that they could decode the metaphor. But a child looks at an image like that and accepts what they see. They respond literally and emotionally. They don’t interpret, they react.

The same is true of what they are told. When a Sunday School teacher or pastor tells a young child that God sees everything they do and knows what they are thinking it impacts them deeply. They may start to feel like they are under the God microscope. Even their own thoughts are being assessed if those thoughts are naughty or nice.

Fear based religion isn’t just stored as belief. It turns up as actions and emotions. Children who grew up secretly fearing God may feel more guilt and anxiety than considered normal. At one level an adult can say, “I no longer believe God is angry with me.” And yet, at the same time feel their pulse quicken at thoughts of God knowing and judging them. It can be difficult to escape fear based religion, especially if implanted at an early age.

Fear based religion needs a different model than that of the Old Testament God that sent the Death Angel into the homes of ancient Egyptians to kill the oldest male child. 

This is what Jesus is all about. My growing understanding of Him is that He came to show us that God is love. Hey touched the untouchable. He welcomed children. He did not condemn the woman caught in adultery. He ate with those rejected by religion.

What if God is not standing on the clouds watching and waiting for you to fail? What if God is more like Jesus kneeling in the dust beside the accused? 

Some of us have spent decades trying to stop being afraid of a God we met before we were old enough to question Him. That doesn’t make us weak or damaged beyond repair. It means we were kids and we believed what the adults  we trusted told us.

Maybe healing starts when we stop scolding that frightened kid and sit beside him. Tell him you are not being watched for failure. You are being held in love.

title.rendered: The Picture That Made Me Fear God

content.rendered:
The Picture That Made Me Fear God

Every kid forms a picture of God. Mine came from one terrifying illustration in an old family Bible

I was seven years old when I opened my family’s Bible and saw a picture that would shape my view of God for decades.

A large man dressed in a white robe stood on towering gray clouds. Massive stone tablets rested beneath each arm. His long white beard made Him look ancient.

But it wasn’t His beard that frightened me.

It was His eyes. Yellow lightning bolts shot from them.

As I stared at the picture, questions flooded my young mind.

Why did He look so angry?

Church had always taught me that God loved me. But the picture suggested something entirely different. For the first time, I wondered if God was someone to run from instead of someone to run to. 

I couldn’t explain it, but I suddenly felt exposed. I didn’t even know what I had done wrong, but I felt guilty. It seemed as though God had been waiting for me to open the Bible so He could catch me doing something wrong. 

Those eyes followed me on into adulthood.

Looking back, I realize something important. That picture didn’t just change how I looked at God. It changed how I looked at myself.

For years, I lived as though I had to stay on God’s good side. I believed His love depended on my performance. I spent decades trying not to piss Him off.

What I didn’t know was that this scary picture of God would eventually collide with the person of Jesus. That collision would change everything.

Have you ever been afraid of God?

If you’ve ever wondered whether God is disappointed with you or if you’ve ever lived with the fear that you’ll never be good enough you’re not alone.

Those questions launched a journey that took me decades to answer. That’s what A God Awful God: A Memoir of Fear, Faith, and Learning God is Love is all about. 

If this story sounds familiar, I’d love to walk this journey with you. Click the banner above and I’ll send you the first chapter of A God Awful God free. Along the way I’ll share stories, reflections, and updates as the book moves toward publication.

title.rendered: The Preacher Who Sent Himself to Hell

content.rendered:
He stood in front of the room filled with 50 teens like he owned them. Strutting like a peacock back and forth had a hypnotic effect on everyone, including me. His voice was soft and slow but with each word it increased in both speed and volume. I couldn’t believe what he told them. And yet, I said to myself, I’m not surprised.

He told the story of returning home from vacation. He glanced down and noticed the speedometer read 60 MPH. As he looked up the road sign said “Speed Limit 55 MPH.” He gave a dramatic pause and announced, “But I didn’t slow down.” He stopped. Stared at them like a stern father, and asked, “If I had gotten in a car wreck that moment would I have gone to heaven or hell?”

The teens held their breath. Several had a look of panic on their face. After a pause that went on too long, he announced in an angry voice, “I would’ve went straight to hell because the Bible says we should obey the laws of man.”

Teens let the air out of their lungs. Some shifted nervously in their seat. The  blond headed guy in front of me dropped his head and looked at the floor. Two girls turned and looked at each other as though trying to imagine what life in hell would be like. 

There it is. This is the kind of spiritually legalistic abuse many in the church grew up with. And it wasn’t just directed at teens but adults as well. 

Not everyone had this experience but far too many who read this know exactly what I’m talking about.

What if God isn’t like that at all? What if Jesus was right when He announced that God is love?

That kind of God and the fear it generates is at the core of my new book. If you are interested feel free to click on the banner above to discover more about my soon to be released book called A God Awful God: A Memoir of Fear, Faith, and Learning God is Love.

title.rendered: Pot Stirrer or Bridge Builder? Give Me 5 Minutes.

content.rendered:
I’m tired of the division around me. Are you sick of it like I am? People on the right yell at the left, and the left yells at the right  I’m tired. Real tired. We are so busy debating and defending that we have nearly lost our minds. I know there’s a lot at stake.  Maybe the Constitution is about to fall and the world as we know it is hanging by a thread. Maybe you hate Trump or mayne you love him. But just slow down.

I’m asking you to stop and take a deep breath. Can you give me five minutes? That’s all I want.

It’s November 1969 and 540,000 United States soldiers are fighting in the jungles of Viet Nam. The fighting is intense. Young soldiers are getting blown up. As 1969 drew to a close, 11,000 soldiers had lost their lives in that foreign country. Anti-war protests were springing up and tensions were increasing. The nation was facing a crisis and had grown weary.

At this point in time, a guy named Simon wrote a song. His buddy Garfunkel sings the main part of the song and Simon joins in the chorus. Magic happens. During that emotionally charged period of our history the new song, A Bridge Over Troubled Water, started playing on the radio. People driving down the highway with their radios on heard theseopening lines:

“When you’re weary, feeling small,
When tears are in your eyes, I will dry them all; I’m on your side.”

In my imagination I feel their tensions ease. Those words are like a magic tonic.

Then these words come through the car speakers,

“If you need a friend I’m sailing right behind.
Like a bridge over troubled water I will ease your mind.”

In the last week, I’ve played this song, a winner of 5 Grammys, every day. It reminds me that my best work isn’t to be a pot-stirrer but a bridge builder. It’s not a cop out. But it’s the constructive way forward. I don’t know what that looks like for you but anything has got to be better than this constant battling between Americans.

What do you think? Give me 5 minutes. Remove all distractions and listen. Let it calm you. Consider playing this song for the next 30 days before you leave the house. I hope it helps each of us decide to be bridges over troubled water instead of pot-stirrers in order to help heal this broken country.

It’s a small thing but it’s a start. 

Let me know how it works for you.

title.rendered: Holiness and Baloneyness and Gatekeepers

content.rendered:
You can only keep the gates locked until the key shows up. 

Gatekeepers scurried and hurried to strengthen their grip on the little sinking ship.

“Tighten the rules and silence those fools who dare to refuse the mandate of silence!”

As chains tightened and loopholes became less loopy, things became incredibly kooky.

Holiness turned into balonyness, which produced a coronary stoniness, bordering on felonious. 

“Called unto holiness” turned into “stalled in our holiness” and yet the ordained Titanic band played on. 

Gatekeepers kept gating while waiting for voices to be voiceless. 

Pious Dopes in their tower wielded their power, forcing the faithful to undergo trials. 

But you can only keep the gates locked until the key shows up.

Some how and some way the dove, of love swung low, like a sweet chariot. 

Can you hear the distant melody of love, calling from some where over the alphabet rainbow?

Gates, chains and locks will never trump love because love is THE key. 

It flings open the gates of rejection. 

It sets the prisoners free. 

It invites all to the table. 

It topples those in their towers. 

And it turns balonyness back into holiness.

You can’t keep the gates locked because the key of love HAS shown up.

title.rendered: The Church of the Nazarene, The LGBTQ+ Community, and ChatGPT

content.rendered:
This morning I wondered what artificial intelligence would think o the refusal of the Church of the Nazarene to affirm members of the LGBTQ+ community. Here’s what ChatGPT told me:

In the sacred halls where prayers ascend,

A sanctuary, a refuge, a place to mend.

But within these walls, a tale untold,

Of hearts denied, stories left cold.

Oh, Church of the Nazarene, with steeple high,

Why exclude those under the same sky?

Queer souls knocking, seeking embrace,

Yet met with judgment, a closed-off space.

In the pews they sit, shadows in the light,

Yearning for love, acceptance in sight.

But doctrine echoes, rigid and stern,

A barrier erected, a lesson to learn.

Love proclaimed in scriptures divine,

Yet a contradiction, a restrictive line.

A marginalized flock, cast away,

In the name of faith, they silently pray.

But love is boundless, transcends belief,

No exclusion in its vast relief.

Why, then, this refusal to understand,

The beauty of diversity, hand in hand?

In the silence between hymns, a whisper grows,

A plea for acceptance, a challenge to impose.

For Nazarenes to evolve, to redefine,

To cast away judgment, and let love shine.

For in the core of spirituality,

Resides a call for unity, equality.

To love thy neighbor, without condition,

A divine command, a sacred mission.

Let the pulpit resonate with compassion’s tone,

Welcoming all, making love known.

For the queer community, too, seeks grace,

Yearning for a warm and open embrace.

Oh, Church of the Nazarene, hear the plea,

Break the chains of exclusion, set love free.

Embrace the rainbow, let it adorn,

The sacred space where love is reborn.

Artificial intelligence gets it. When will we?

title.rendered: An Open Letter About Dee Kelley to the Board of General Superintendents

content.rendered:
Dear Board of General Superintendents (David Busic, Gustavo Crocker, Fili Chambo, Carla Sunberg, Scott Daniels, and Christian Sarmiento),
 
I stand with Dee Kelley.
 
I’m shocked you allowed charges to be filed against this exemplary pastor. I’m stunned his credentials were stripped. I’m angry he was denied an appeal to that decision.
I stand with Dee Kelley.
Your silence is telling but it shouldn’t surprise me. You set the stage for it to happen. Two years ago I faced the same charges as Dee. But at my trial, three people recognized I had not taught doctrine out of harmony with the church. Why? Because our doctrine consisted of the Articles of Faith. As you know, there is NOTHING in those articles about the LGBTQ+ community. This is 100% the reason the trial failed to strip me of my credentials and I’m still an ordained elder.
 
So what did you, the Board of General Superintendents, do? You redefined “doctrine” as the Articles of Faith + the Code of Christian Conduct + the Code of Christian Character. These other documents contain a reference to marriage as being between a man and a woman. But those two documents were never viewed as “doctrine.” With that change, charges of “teaching doctrine contrary to our doctrine” have more teeth.
 
By including these two documents in the definition of doctrine you created ammunition to win trials like mine and force elders out.
 
So now, it’s open season on pastors who believe God’s affirming love extends to everyone. Rev. Dr. Dee Kelley is your latest victim. You and I know there are other pastors being threatened with a trial for affirming members of the LGBTQ+ community.
 
I stand with Dee Kelley.
 
This is a dark day in our denomination. And it not only happened on your watch, it happened because of you.
 
If you feel no shame, I’m ashamed for you. If you shed no tears, I weep for you. If your heart doesn’t ache over what you’ve done, mine aches for you.
I urge you to make this right. Lead us in the right direction. Set the example for true holiness.
 
I stand with Dee Kelley.
 
Sincerely,
 
Rev. Dr. Randall Hartman

title.rendered: Will THIS Hypocrisy Doom the Church of the Nazarene?

content.rendered:
My support of the LGBTQ+ community is no secret. I’ve written about my trial and shared other articles about the culture of fear emerging in the Church of the Nazarene. The situation is not improving. Last month, the ecclesiastical machinery defrocked pastor Dee Kelley over the LGBTQ+ debate. Even as I write, they are moving toward filing charges against other pastors for similar reasons.
 
HAVE YOU NOTICED THE BLATANT HYPOCRISY IN WHAT IS HAPPENING?
 
Consider that the Articles of Faith (AOF) mention nothing about the LGBTQ+ community. But there is a clear Nazarene AOF about Scripture. Our view of Scripture isn’t casually mentioned or alluded to. It is specific and the entire AOF spells out how a Nazarene should view the Bible. See for yourself:
 
“We believe in the plenary inspiration of the Holy Scriptures, by which we understand the 66 books of the Old and New Testaments, given by divine inspiration, inerrantly revealing the will of God concerning us in all things necessary to our salvation, so that whatever is not contained therein is not to be enjoined as an article of faith.” (Manual 2017-2021, Church of the Nazarene)
 
Think of the phrase, …”inerrantly revealing the will of God concerning us in all things necessary to our salvation,” We believe the Bible is spot on when it comes to getting us to heaven. Our AOF regarding Scripture doesn’t teach that the Bible is a history book or science book. To say, “The Bible is either all true or it isn’t” is a statement contrary to the AOF. 
 
In spite of this, many ordained Nazarene pastors teach and proclaim the doctrine of inerrancy. This is not news. These pastor who teach contrary to the AOF about Scripture go uncheck.
  • They don’t worry about getting a certified letter from their District Superintendent informing them charges were filed against them.
  • They don’t stay awake at night worried about getting fired.
  • They don’t parse their words on Facebook for fear of screenshots being sent to their District Superintendent.
ZERO ordained elders who teach inerrancy have been charged with “teaching doctrine contrary to the Church of the Nazarene.” And yet, this is exactly what they are doing. Why are they given a pass?
 
For example, last week the subject of inerrancy was debated on a Facebook group devoted to Nazarene theology. An ordained elder on the Iowa District, who pastors a hispanic work, defended his belief in inerrancy. He added that he has taught this doctrine for twenty years. He went on to assert that his district superintendent and most pastors on the district share his view about Scripture. And yet, no one has brought charges against him. Odd, since he is in a teaching role and teaching contrary to an AOF.
 
Are you seeing the hypocrisy in our denomination and the leaders?
 
Our failure as a denomination isn’t that we still have LGBTQ+ affirming pastors. No. Our failure as a denomination is that we have failed to defend our position about AOF #4.
This failure is as devastating as the results of the Titanic hitting the iceberg. Unless the Board of General Superintendents correct this failure, our denomination may sink into the icy waters of oblivion.
 
If you think this is making an iceberg out of an icecube it can only mean you don’t get it. But I wish you would. I wish you could grasp that it isn’t the debate about affirming pastors we need to focus on. If we are going to bring charges against pastors and drag their butts through a church trial let it be for teaching doctrine contrary to AOF #4. This is where the battle for the heart and soul of our denomination should focus.
 
Why aren’t gatekeepers focused on the real problem in our church? I don’t understand. But I recognize hypocrisy when I see it.
 
Meanwhile, the band on the deck plays Holiness Unto the Lord while some gatekeeprs search for affirming pastors to put on trial.
 
I hope we’ve not taken on too much water and that the Church of the Nazarene can be saved.

title.rendered: It’s 4:09 AM, But Somewhere Last Night…

content.rendered:
It’s 4:09 AM, But Somewhere Last Night…

Somewhere last night:

  • a Nazarene pastor, only guilty of holy love, received news his career was over.
  • the devil smiled and demons danced.
  • accusers slapped each other on the back and hummed, “We are a glorious church without spot or wrinkle.”
  • a smoldering dumpster fire became a consuming fire.
  • old clergy wondered why they had spent their lives in the belly of the beast.
  • young clergy contemplated their escape plans.
  • relieved gatekeepers congratulated the committee for doing what had to be done.
  • 100 hymns about love were deleted from the hymnal.
  • the doomsday clock in the Church of the Nazarene ticked another minute closer to midnight.

But somewhere last night:

  • Jesus wept and the God of love had His heart broken again.
  • loving Nazarenes joined their voices with the ancients by the River of Babylon and “wept when we remembered Zion.”
  • we wished Nazarenes still focused on saving, not destroying.
  • we wanted to keep believing that love still wins and evil won’t.
  • love took a hit and faltered, reeled, moved to the back pew.
  • God reminded us He IS love.
  • And out of the darkness the love of God will shine even brighter.
  • I want to believe. Lord help my unbelief.

Randall Hartman

title.rendered: Why Don’t You Just Leave the Denomination? Here’s Why.

content.rendered:
As a pastor I’ve counseled couples in crisis. One day a couple stopped into the office looking for help. Their thirty year marriage was in jeopardy. On their wedding day they exchanged vows to stay together. This couple had children and grandchildren. They had given their lives to each other. They were heavily invested in each other. And yet, here they were, struggling with a major disagreement. Through the recent election cycle, one voted Republican, the other Democrat. The disagreement between the two was like a deep chasm. After listening to their story, I took a deep breath. Here’s what I told them.

“You two should get a divorce. Leave each other. It’s clear. You are no longer in love. Why are you putting up with each other? Go find someone else to love and spend the rest of your life with.”

Isn’t that a stupid thing to say to this couple? Do you think after the love and life they’ve shared they should split because of one disagreement?

Okay. You got me. I made up the whole story. But I’m making a point.

In the last couple of years I’ve lost count of how many people who asked, “Why do you stay in the Church of the Nazarene?” Others are a little more direct and demand I leave. Why? Because I have become affirming of members in the queer community. The church and I disagree on this one issue which isn’t even addressed by any of the Articles of Faith.

I’m 69 years old. I attended my first Nazarene service when I was three days old. The family I was born into made me a fifth generation Nazarene. Grandpa was a Nazarene preacher. I graduated from Olivet Nazarene University and Nazarene Theological Seminary. At a District Assembly, leaders ordained me by the laying on of hands into ministry. I served as a pastor for 35 years in the denomination. I’ve invested my life into the church that I love.

And now, after one disagreement, you think I should leave? That’s like suggesting to the ficticious couple they split and go find someone else to love. It’s crass and cruel. It’s silly and thoughtless. And, in a moment of weakness, I confess that it’s hurtful.

So why am I staying? I’m staying because I’m in love with the Church of the Nazarene. She’s been the only church love I’ve ever known. We’ve held hands together. We exchanged vows. We’ve walked through deep waters side by side. Together we’ve wept and laughed through decades of ministry.

You want me to walk away from the church I love? I guess you don’t know me very well. Nope. I’m not leaving. I’m staying, even if we disagree on one issue. Who knows? Maybe the church and I can work things out. Or how about this:

How about we agree to disagree and get on with the real business of the church?

That’s my answer. And I’m sticking to it. How about you?

title.rendered: My Biggest Surprise about the LGBTQ+ from the 2023 Nazarene General Assembly

content.rendered:
Every four years, friends and delegates gather from around the world for the Nazarene General Assembly. At this assembly they conduct business and enjoy times of worship. This General Assembly is the mother of all Church of the Nazarene meetings. In these meetings it’s possible to intiate changes to the rules and belief statements of the church. It’s a week of high powered holiness injection for attendees.

If you attended, were you surprised at:

  • the huge number of Nazarenes wandering around with lanyards around their necks?
  • that during the election of General Superintendents, gossip spread to keep a candidate from getting elected?
  • at the cost of food in the Convention Center?

None of those things surprised me. But I was surprised at the level of support for the full inclusion of the LGBTQ+ into the church. This support was not spoken in meetings or displayed on signs. Nope. People who I didn’t know but must be readers of my articles, flashed me a thumbs up or shared words of encouragement. It occurred to me an increasing number of laypeople are fully affirming of queer people. This leads to an interesting question.

What will denominational leaders do when people in the pew find their affirming voice? So far the strategy from the top down is to silence affirming clergy. Pastors are threatened into silence or face the consequences. As an example, pastors face the possible loss of ministerial credentials through a process ending in a trial. But what happens when the laity begin to champion full inclusion of the LGBTQ+ community? What happens when board members insist a married lesbian couple be granted church membership? Of course the pastor can put a stop to it. But do you think the board members will let it go?

How will they silence these growing number of voices? It won’t work to threaten them with the with loss of ministerial credentials. Will they face a trial? Will the pastor remove them from leadership positions? Perhaps. But it won’t silence the increasing number of people who believe that God’s love is for everyone.

Now that they are finding their voices, they won’t be quiet. They won’t quit. They won’t back down. Affirming people are in this for the long haul. After all, time is on their side.

title.rendered: Rick Warren’s Recent Confession, the LGBTQ+ and the Church of the Nazarene

content.rendered:
Did it ever occur to you that when it comes to the LGBTQ+ community you might be wrong?
From childhood, you’ve been taught that members of the queer community are hell-bound. Your pastor, Sunday School teacher, and Church all warned you of the dire fate awaiting those who dared fall in love with members of the same sex. If you started to doubt that position, you were assured “the Bible says it’s wrong.” And so, here you are in the Church of the Nazarene, with a stance that demeans people in the queer community.
 
That brings us to the recent confession of Rev. Rick Warren, the founder of Saddleback Community Church. He is arguably the most influential member of the Southern Baptist Church. In that denomination women are not permitted to preach or lead. But in 2021 Warren’s church ordained three women into ministry. As a result the Southern Baptist Convention kicked Saddleback Community out of the Southern Baptist fold.
 
As those events were unfolding, Rick Warren released an apology to women.
 
“My biggest regret in 53 years of ministry is that I didn’t do my own personal exegesis sooner on the 4 passages used to restrict women. Shame on me. I wasted those 4 yrs of Greek in college & seminary. When I finally did my proper ‘due diligence’, laying aside 50 years of bias, I was shocked, chagrined, and embarrassed… I think maybe it was because I didn’t WANT to know anything that might challenge the view I WANTED to believe for 50 yrs.”
 
You can find Rick’s full statement on his Twitter page.
 
As I followed these events, I saw myself in this story. But my issue wasn’t with women in ministry, it was with the people who were part of the LGBTQ+ community. In my more than sixty years in the church I was taught about the evils of the this community. And because I heard it from people I respected and trusted I never bothered to study and think through those issues for myself. Like Warren, “I didn’t WANT to know anything that might challenge the view I WANTED to believe” my entire life. It was only when I decided to do my own study of Scripture that I changed my mind and fully embraced the LGBTQ+ community.
 
Rick Warren’s story is not the same as mine. But do you see there is an applicable principle in the current stand of the Church of the Nazarene about the queer community? Study the Scriptures for yourself. Think for yourself. Read books on the subject. But most of all seek the heart of God. You may not change your mind, but we will still be friends, right?
 
Warren, in his apology to women, asked for forgiveness.
 
“I PUBLICLY APOLOGIZE to every good women in my life, church, and ministry that I failed to speak up for in my years of ignorance. What grieves me is that I hindered them in obeying the Great Commission command (And Acts 2:17-18) that EVERYONE is to TEACH in the church. I held them back from using the spiritual gifts and leadership skills that the Holy Spirit had sovereignly placed in them. That breaks my heart now, and I am truly repentant and sorry for my sin. I wish I could do it all over. Christian women, will you please forgive me?”
 
As I reflect on this paragraph, I recognize there were times in my 40 years of ministry that I failed to stand up for the LGBTQ+ community. I failed to even study the subject myself; content to play follow the leader. As I tearfully type these words I publicly apologize to every member of the gay community. My silence and lack of caring has done you harm. I’m so sorry and I repent. I accept you. I love you. I affirm you.
 
Members of the LGBTQ+ family, will you please forgive me?

Update: As part of my affirmation of the gay community I ended up facing a church trial. The journey from fear to love is the theme of my upcoming memoir: A God Awful Gog: The God I Feared Wasn’t The God I Found. If you want to know more about the book and read the first chapter just enter your email adress.
